newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Czech rates to be high for some time-CNB official.
newsitem.headline: Czech rates to be high for some time-CNB official.

text.p: Czech interest rates will remain at higher levels for some time to protect the crown from more speculative attacks which prompted recent hasty rate hikes, a senior central bank official said.

"We still support the exchange rate through relatively high-term interest rates," Miroslav Hrncir, a member of the Czech National Bank's board, told Reuters Financial Television in an interview late on Sunday.

Massive speculative attacks on the Czech crown in late May, triggered by a high current account deficit, forced the central bank to intervene in the currency market and hike interest rates quite dramatically to prop up the sagging currency.
And while the central bank last week took its first steps toward easing rates, Hrncir predicted the process of reducing rates again would be quite measured.
"We are trying to decrease them (short term rates) but only step by step. That means that it will take some time," he said.

The central bank last week cut its repo rate to a still high 45 percent after having hastily pushed it to 75 percent earlier. But the Lombard emergency borrowing rate remains at 50 percent, up from the 14.9 percent rate seen in early May.
Hrncir justified the bank's rate policies, saying they were imperative to keep speculators at bay.
"Just to stabilise the currency, it is necessary to live for some period with the higher interest rate."

Even as a cautious practice of normalising rates has been started, Hrncir said "I cannot expect rates to return to previous levels," and predicted rates could remain at higher levels for another month.
Economic fallout from the turmoil is likely to be limited, however, Hrncir predicted, saying the central bank expected to keep inflation under control.

"We must expect some feedback from the change in the currency rate but at the same time we would not like to have the inflation level increase considerably beyond 10 percent," he said, adding "We would be satisfied if we could remain in this one digit region."
The Czech Republic posted single-digit inflation rates during the past two years, with inflation standing around eight percent in 1996.
Looking ahead Hrncir still expects a steady decline in inflation, saying "our expectations would be for a one percent drop in inflation per year. That would be quite an achievement."
A positive effect of the softer currency could be that it may sharpen Czech competitiveness and help stop the foreign trade account deterioration, Hrncir said.

"The change in the exchange rate could help us be more competitive," he said predicting also "we certainly believe that the trade account should not deteriorate any more. We expect some sort of stabilisation of the present level and perhaps even some improvement."
Hrncir said it might now be possible to register a rise in exports of higher valued added products allowing the Czech Republic to shift away from relying mostly on an export of raw materials.
